--- title: "Between-Unit vs. Within-Unit Effects" --- # Between-Unit vs. Within-Unit Effects ## The Same Variable, Two Stories Consider studying whether a nation's GDP predicts its citizens' wellbeing. You have survey data from 60 countries over 10 years. **The between-country question:** Do richer countries have happier citizens on average? **The within-country question:** In years when a country's GDP grows, do its citizens report higher wellbeing? These are completely different empirical questions. The between-country question picks up all stable differences between rich and poor countries (culture, institutions, climate, history). The within-country question is closer to a causal estimate of the effect of economic growth on wellbeing, net of these stable differences. Research consistently finds that the answers are *different*: rich countries are happier than poor ones, but within a country, economic booms correlate with wellbeing only modestly (the "Easterlin Paradox"). ## Separating the Effects: The Mundlak Device The cleanest way to separate within- and between-unit effects is to include both in the same model: 1. Cluster-mean center the predictor (captures within-unit variation) 2. Include the cluster mean as a separate level-2 predictor (captures between-unit variation) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Simulate country panel data n_countries <- 40 n_years <- 10 # Between: rich countries ARE happier (partly for other reasons) country_gdp_avg <- rnorm(n_countries, 50, 15) country_wellbeing_base <- 50 + 0.6 * country_gdp_avg + rnorm(n_countries, 0, 8) # Within: growth has only modest effect on wellbeing df_gdp <- expand_grid(country = 1:n_countries, year = 1:n_years) |> mutate( gdp_raw = country_gdp_avg[country] + rnorm(n(), 0, 5), wellbeing = country_wellbeing_base[country] + 0.15 * (gdp_raw - country_gdp_avg[country]) + rnorm(n(), 0, 4), country = factor(country) ) |> group_by(country) |> mutate( gdp_mean = mean(gdp_raw), gdp_cmc = gdp_raw - gdp_mean ) |> ungroup() # Pooled (mixes effects) m_pooled <- lmer(wellbeing ~ gdp_raw + (1 | country), data = df_gdp) # Mundlak: both within and between m_mundlak <- lmer(wellbeing ~ gdp_cmc + gdp_mean + (1 | country), data = df_gdp) bind_rows( broom.mixed::tidy(m_pooled, effects = "fixed") |> mutate(model = "Pooled"), broom.mixed::tidy(m_mundlak, effects = "fixed") |> mutate(model = "Mundlak") ) |> select(model, term, estimate, std.error, p.value) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Within vs. between effects of GDP on wellbeing") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Within vs. between effects of GDP on wellbeing |model |term | estimate| std.error| p.value| |:-------|:-----------|--------:|---------:|-------:| |Pooled |(Intercept) | 68.115| 2.565| 0| |Pooled |gdp_raw | 0.252| 0.039| 0| |Mundlak |(Intercept) | 45.994| 4.371| 0| |Mundlak |gdp_cmc | 0.187| 0.041| 0| |Mundlak |gdp_mean | 0.683| 0.082| 0| ::: ::: The Mundlak model reveals: - **Within effect (gdp_cmc ≈ 0.15):** When a country's GDP is above its own average, wellbeing is modestly higher. Small effect. - **Between effect (gdp_mean ≈ 0.6):** Countries with higher average GDP have substantially higher wellbeing — but this partly reflects other stable advantages of wealthy nations. The pooled model blends these two stories into one coefficient that misrepresents both. ## The Assumption Test: Are Within and Between Effects Equal? The formal test for whether within and between effects are equal is simple: if the CMC model's within coefficient ($\beta_{within}$) and between coefficient ($\beta_{between}$) are statistically indistinguishable, you can use the simpler pooled model. If they differ, they must be separated. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(car) # Test: within effect = between effect? linearHypothesis(m_mundlak, "gdp_cmc = gdp_mean") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Df| Chisq| Pr(>Chisq)| |--:|--------:|----------:| | NA| NA| NA| | 1| 29.48468| 1e-07|
::: ::: A significant test (p < 0.05) means within and between effects differ — the pooled model is misspecified.
